new_statements.rule_in_words: Southern Thai is a tone language in which every syllable carries a lexical tone; stress is not contrastive. Within a polysyllabic morpheme, a compound or a reduplicate, the non-final syllable(s) are stress-reduced (first degree: vowel quality kept, length neutralised, sandhi tone; second/extreme degree: final consonant lost, vowel becomes short /a/, all tonal contrast lost = 'neutral tone'), while the final syllable is fully stressed and carries the canonical tone. Prominence is therefore rightmost/final within the word or close-knit phrase. Diller 1989 (Sathing Phra, Songkhla) independently states that stress 'should be considered secondary or non-contrastive' and that unmarked syllables are 'unstressed variable-pitch' (neutral-tone-like) syllables; Diller 1979a notes that initial syllables of bisyllabic lexemes are 'lightly-accented' and are regularly deleted (apheresis) in rural Southern Thai.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed as such; Court distinguishes only fully stressed vs. two degrees of non-fully stressed syllables.
new_statements.exceptions: Court: a few Malay loanwords with irregular (non-sandhi) tones in penult (p.73). Diller 1989: stress features of deictic Groups II and IV are variable; Group I deictics form the stress peak of the utterance.
new_statements.domain_note: Court describes stress reduction within polysyllabic morphemes (mostly Malay loans), compounds, reduplicates and 'close-knit phrases' — i.e. word/phonological-phrase level, not citation monosyllables; Diller 1989's remarks are about deictic words in connected speech.
new_statements.identity_note: The deciding source (Court 1975) describes Satun Thai, the Southern Thai dialect of Satun province spoken by ethnically Malay speakers on the western coast, which Court calls 'a typical Pak Tai (southern Thai) dialect'; Diller 1989 describes the Sathing Phra (Songkhla) rural dialect; Diller 1979a covers rural vs. urban Southern Thai generally. All fall under sout2746 (no separate glottocode for Satun or Songkhla Thai). Glottolog's Saiegh-Haddad 2011 reference is a misattribution (Arabic).

sources.note: Satun Thai (a 'typical Pak Tai' dialect): tones a-n occur in fully stressed syllables, sandhi tones o-s in non-fully-stressed syllables before a fully stressed one (p.70); section 'Tone sandhi and stress reduction' (p.72): first element of a compound or reduplicate is stress-reduced, two degrees of reduction (2nd degree = vowel to short /a/, all tone lost, 'neutral tone'); non-final syllables of polysyllabic morphemes are subject to stress reduction (p.73). Stress itself is not treated as contrastive.

sources.note: Sathing Phra (Songkhla) Southern Thai: 'Absence of a subscript [tone number] indicates an unstressed variable-pitch syllable, not unlike the so-called neutral tone of Mandarin Chinese' (p.2); 'stress in this dialect should be considered secondary or non-contrastive' — Group I deictics always fully stressed and usually the stress peak of the utterance, Group III postclitics regularly unstressed (p.4); decreasing stress codes the deictic series (p.11).
